title: Rich in Cattle, Rich in Truth
hook: a cowshed at dawn, jasmine on the door, eight Lakshmis, and a hymn that counts truth of speech as riches
tomorrow: why does Lakshmi always sit on a lotus?

segments.voice: Yesterday gave misfortune a face, Alakshmi, and the singer helped show her the door: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in.

A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth. Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe. Every one of those smells means the household is alive: fuel, food, animals fed, someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning. The riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.
screen: `WOODSMOKE, WET EARTH, WARM MILK.` → `THE COWSHED, AND JASMINE.` → `A HOUSEHOLD THAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance. She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung. It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household, dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields and plaster for the floor. It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line. In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me. First it asks for things nobody can store in a barn: an intention carried through, truth in what you say. In a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches. And this is what Hindus mean when they say Lakshmi is more than money. A popular later hymn praises eight Lakshmis, the Ashta Lakshmi: wealth, yes, but also grain, courage, children, knowledge and victory among them. In village homes, cows are honored at Diwali, and floors are freshly plastered before the puja. The fortune this hymn wants is wider than a bank balance, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.
screen: `HER DOORWAY IS FRAGRANCE.` · `RICH IN COW DUNG, QUEEN OF ALL.` · `THE WISH, THE INTENTION, THE TRUTH.` · `EIGHT LAKSHMIS.` · then, large: `TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.`

segments.voice: Count your riches the way the eight Lakshmis do, one per breath: food today, a roof, someone who's family to you, a bit of courage, something you know, a small win. Then turn inward: an intention you've been carrying, something true you said this week, and let that count too. If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for each; if you don't, let yourself be a little richer than you thought.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that calls Sri fragrant at the door and rich in cow dung, and asks for truth of speech in the same breath as cattle and food.
Your line: Lakshmi is more than money. Jasmine at the door, the cowshed out back, and an honest word. I'll be here tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1098 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES LAKSHMI ALWAYS SIT ON A LOTUS?`

howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

karishini.meaning: rich in cow dung, a sign of a thriving farm

Sri Sukta.meaning: the hymn to Sri, the goddess of fortune

Ashta Lakshmi.meaning: the eight Lakshmis: eight forms of fortune

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 9–10 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 9 paraphrased: gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm / īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ tām ihopahvaye śriyam. karīṣiṇī glossed 'rich in cow dung' (karīṣa, dried dung); some translators soften it to 'abounding in cattle wealth'. Confirm the plain rendering is acceptable for this audience.
Verse 10 paraphrased: manasaḥ kāmam ākūtiṃ vācaḥ satyam aśīmahi / paśūnāṃ rūpam annasya mayi śrīḥ śrayatāṃ yaśaḥ. ākūti glossed 'intention of the heart'; yaśas as 'good name'. Confirm.
Uses of dung (fuel, fertilizer, floor plaster) are given as everyday rural practice, not tied to the text; confirm.
The two readings (outer and inner household; a full life described from the ground up) are offered without ranking.
